newsitem.title: CANADA: Ukraine's prime minister sees economic growth.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's prime minister sees economic growth.

text.p: Ukrainian Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, visiting Canada to promote investment in his country, on Friday predicted slight growth in gross domestic product and lower inflation over the next year.
Lazarenko said he expected Ukraine's inflation for 1997 would not exceed 11 or 12 percent. He also expected GDP growth of about one percent, after a 10.5 percent drop in 1996.
"We have very nice plants. We have unique production lines and people who are very interested in investment," he told the National Press Club.

But Lazarenko was confronted by the issue of corruption in the Ukraine business community after a front-page article this week in Toronto's influential Globe and Mail newspaper about allegations of corruption surrounding the prime minister.
"Do we have any shortcomings? Of course we have," he said. "Do we have corruption? Yes, corruption is everywhere to a certain extent."
But he said corruption in Ukraine was exaggerated by his political opponents trying to undermine his government ahead of elections expected in nine months.

Lazarenko met with Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien on Thursday night and will spend the next few days travelling across Canada to promote trade and investment. About 500,000 people of Ukrainian descent live in Canada, the first Western country to recognise Ukraine after its declaration of independence in December 1991.

Trade between the two countries has since grown. Canada's exports to the Ukraine totalled about C$37.7 million ($27.4 million), an increase of about 26 percent since 1993, the Canadian government said. Ukrainian imports from Canada in 1996 were worth C$16.4 million ($11.9 million), up 5 percent since 1993.

Lazarenko also used his speaking engagement in Ottawa to thank Russian President Boris Yeltsin for settling the longstanding issue of the former Soviet Black Sea Fleet based at Ukraine's Crimean peninsula.
"The government of Ukraine is sincerely thankful to Boris Yeltsin ... for the resolution of this issue," Lazarenko said. "The decisions completely satisfied both Ukraine and Russia."
